questions.q: How do a scheduler and a queue share the work in the Task API?
questions.explain: The scheduler starts work because of the time. The queue from the background jobs lesson makes the work reliable. Used together, the scheduler only has to add a job at the right moment.
options: The queue decides when work runs; the scheduler retries it
The scheduler decides when; the queue makes sure the work gets done, with retries and dead letters
They do the same job, so you pick one of them
The scheduler replaces the queue once you have cron

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: No job called refresh-stats was defined, so scheduling it throws at once. The lesson's rule: scheduling an id you never defined throws. The duration "5m" itself is fine.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A job id names one function. Defining the same id twice is refused, so two parts of the app cannot silently replace each other's job. One job can still have several schedules.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: every returns a handle, a remote control for that one schedule. It is active as soon as it is created, pause() makes it paused, and cancel() ends it for good.

questions.q: Where should the Task API call scheduler.stop()?
questions.explain: stop() ends the timers and deals with running jobs. Call it on shutdown next to the queue workers, so a deploy does not cut a job off halfway without warning.
options: Nowhere; the scheduler stops when the process exits
After every run, so timers do not pile up
In the shutdown code, in the same place that stops the queue workers

questions.q: You need "once, 30 seconds from now". Which call is it?
questions.explain: after runs once after a delay. every would repeat every 30 seconds, at takes a Date, and the cron expression means minute 30 of every hour.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Durations are turned into milliseconds. 90 s is 90 000 ms, 1 h 30 m is 90 minutes (5 400 000 ms), and 2 d is 48 hours (172 800 000 ms). Units can be combined, as in 1h30m.
questions.code:
import { parseDuration } from "@zudojs/scheduler";

console.log(parseDuration("90s"), parseDuration("1h30m"), parseDuration("2d"));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A bare number is rejected, because nobody can tell whether 5 means seconds or minutes. Always write the unit: "5s" or "5m".

questions.q: What are the five fields of a cron expression, in order?
questions.explain: Minute comes first, which is why 0 9 * * 1-5 means "minute 0, hour 9". Getting minute and hour swapped is the most common cron mistake.
options: second, minute, hour, day of month, month
hour, minute, day of week, month, day of month
minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week
day of week, month, day of month, hour, minute

questions.q: What does 30 2 * * 1-5 mean?
questions.explain: Minute 30, hour 2, any day of the month, any month, day of week 1 to 5. Day of week counts 0 as Sunday, so 1-5 is Monday to Friday.
options: Every 30 minutes on the 2nd of each month
At 02:30 on the 1st to the 5th of the month

questions.q: Which expression runs at minutes 0, 15, 30 and 45 of every hour?
questions.explain: */15 means "every 15th". 15 * * * * runs only at minute 15, * 15 * * * runs every minute from 15:00 to 15:59, and 0-15 runs at each of minutes 0 to 15.

questions.q: Friday 2 October 2026, 12:00 UTC. What does this print?
questions.explain: 09:00 on Friday has already passed at 12:00. Saturday 3 and Sunday 4 are not in 1-5, so the next run is Monday 5 October at 09:00.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 12:00 matches */15, but the next run is always strictly after the date you give. So the answer is 12:15.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: */6 in the hour field is hours 0, 6, 12 and 18, at minute 0. 12:00 is not strictly after 12:00, so the runs are 18:00, then 00:00 of the next day, then 06:00.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: @monthly is a shortcut for 0 0 1 * *: midnight on the 1st. 1 October has already passed, so the next one is 1 November.

questions.q: Both day fields are set. Starting from Friday 2 October 2026, what does this print?
questions.explain: When both day fields are set, cron runs when either matches. So this runs on every Friday (9, 16 October) and on the 13th (a Tuesday). It does not mean "Friday the 13th".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Four fields cannot be parsed, so the first fails with CronParseError. 0 0 30 2 * is valid cron, but 30 February never comes, so the schedule is refused with InvalidScheduleError. Both fail when you write them, not at 2 a.m.

questions.q: Which time zone does the lesson recommend for cron schedules on servers, and why?
questions.explain: Servers move between regions, and local time has daylight-saving gaps and repeats. UTC never jumps. For users who want 09:00 their time, store their zone and compute the UTC time.
options: The server's local zone, because it matches the office
UTC, because it never jumps for daylight saving and is the same on every server
Any named zone, such as "Africa/Lagos", because the package converts it

questions.q: A job is scheduled at 02:30 local time. On the night the clocks jump forward, what happens?
questions.explain: When clocks jump forward (say from 02:00 to 03:00), 02:30 local time never happens, so the job is skipped. When they jump back, 02:30 happens twice. UTC has neither problem.
options: It is skipped, because 02:30 does not exist that night

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The package carries no time-zone database, so named zones are refused rather than silently ignored. It supports only "UTC" or the system local zone.

questions.q: Why does the lesson pass a clock to new Scheduler({ clock }) in its examples?
questions.explain: The clock is where the scheduler reads the current time. A clock that always says 12:00 on 2 October makes every answer predictable, which is how you test schedules.
options: The scheduler cannot tell the time without one
A fixed clock makes nextRun() give the same answer on every computer, so schedules can be tested without waiting

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: every("5m") first runs 5 minutes after now. The clock says 12:00, so the next run is 12:05.

questions.q: A schedule that runs every 5 minutes is paused for 15 minutes, then resumed. What happens?
questions.explain: Resuming computes the next run from now. A schedule paused over three fire times does not fire three times at once.
options: It fires three times at once to catch up
It computes the next run from now; the missed fire times are not replayed
It stays paused until the next day
It throws, because fire times were missed

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A cancelled schedule has no next run, and listSchedules() no longer shows it. Only the stats schedule is left.

questions.q: A job has retry: { attempts: 3 }. It throws on attempts 1 and 2 and works on attempt 3. What does onError receive?
questions.explain: onError hears only about what still fails after the last retry. Here the third attempt worked, so the run is recorded as completed.
options: Two errors, one per failed attempt
Nothing, because the job succeeded in the end
One error, for the first failure

questions.q: A job with timeout: 50 runs for 150 ms. What must the handler do to really stop?
questions.explain: JavaScript cannot kill a running function. The scheduler aborts ctx.signal and reports a SchedulerJobTimeoutError, but the handler has to look at the signal and stop its own work.
options: Nothing; the scheduler kills the function
Check ctx.signal and pass it on to fetch and database calls

questions.q: What should the Task API's onError callback do?
questions.explain: A nightly job can fail every night for a month without anyone noticing. Sending failures to the logs and to an alert makes them visible. The history only holds the last 100 runs and lives in memory.
options: Log the failure with the logger and raise an alert

questions.q: A cleanup runs every 10 minutes but one run takes 25 minutes. Which overlap policy is usually right for it?
questions.explain: "skip" drops fire times while a run is still going. "allow" (the default) lets runs pile up, each one slowing the database further. "replace" would abort the long cleanup every time, so it might never finish.
options: "allow", so no work is ever lost
"skip", because the running cleanup will do the work anyway
"replace", to restart the cleanup every 10 minutes

questions.q: Only the newest result matters: a slow run should be aborted and a fresh one started. Which policy fits?
questions.explain: "replace" aborts the running one and starts fresh. "queue" would wait for the old run and then start one more.

questions.q: The scheduler keeps schedules in memory. After a restart, how does the Task API get its weekday digest back?
questions.explain: Recurring schedules live in your code, which is the source of truth, so nothing is lost. Only schedules that users create, such as reminders, must be stored in the database.
options: It is lost until someone adds it again by hand
The scheduler reloads it from disk
The digest is defined in code when the app starts, every time it starts

questions.q: A user asks "remind me on 12 October at 08:00". Where should that reminder live so it survives a restart?
questions.explain: A user-created reminder is data. Store it in the database and schedule it again on start. (A delayed job on a stored queue is often even simpler for one-off work.)
options: In the database; on start the app reads the rows and schedules them again

questions.q: The server was down at 08:00. The app restores the reminder at 12:00. What does this print?
questions.explain: The reminder's time already passed while the server was down. With misfire: "run-once" (the default) it runs once, right away, which is 12:00 on this clock.

questions.q: Three copies of the Task API run behind a load balancer, each with its own scheduler. What happens at 09:00 without any protection?
questions.explain: Each scheduler is independent and only knows its own process. You need one of the fixes: run it on one instance, take a shared lock, or only enqueue and let an idempotent worker drop duplicates.
options: Only the first copy sends the digest
Each copy sends the digest, so users get it three times
The schedulers notice each other and pick one

questions.q: Why is a queue deduplicationKey alone not enough to stop a second digest?
questions.explain: If server B fires a moment after server A's job has finished, the key no longer blocks it. An idempotent processor, backed by a unique column in the database, protects you no matter when the duplicate arrives.
options: The queue ignores keys made from dates
It only refuses a duplicate while the first job is still in the queue; after it finishes, the same key is accepted again
It refuses every job with a key

questions.q: In the enqueue pattern, why is the day taken from ctx.scheduledAt rather than from new Date()?
questions.explain: The day must be the same for both servers so the duplicate is recognised. The time the run was due is the same on both; the real clock might already be past midnight on one of them.
options: new Date() does not work in handlers
scheduledAt is when the run was due, so two servers that fire a few ms apart get the same day

questions.q: Which item belongs on the production checklist for scheduled work?
questions.explain: A short handler that only enqueues gives the real work the queue's retries and dead letters. The checklist also says: UTC, overlap: "skip", timeouts with ctx.signal, and stop() on shutdown.
options: Write cron expressions in the server's local time
Keep handlers short and put heavy work on a queue
Never call stop(), so runs are not interrupted

questions.q: For a daily cron rule M H * * * in UTC, finish nextDaily(minute, hour, from): return the next run strictly after from as a Date. Build today's run time with Date.UTC; if it is not after from, add one day. The program should print 2026-10-02T23:45:00.000Z and then 2026-10-03T02:30:00.000Z.
questions.explain: 23:45 today is still ahead of 12:00, so it is the answer. 02:30 today has passed, so the run moves to tomorrow. Use <=: the next run is always strictly after from. Working in UTC means no daylight-saving surprises.

questions.q: Write a small toMs(text) like the scheduler's parseDuration, for one number and one unit: ms, s, m or h. Return the milliseconds. For text without a known unit (such as "5"), throw an Error with the message no unit. The program should print 250 30000 300000 3600000 and then no unit.
questions.explain: A regular expression reads the number and the unit, and a lookup table turns the unit into a factor. Put ms before m and s in the pattern (or anchor it with $) so "250ms" is not read as minutes. A missing unit is an error, never a guess.

questions.q: Finish matches(field, value) for one cron field. Support * (any value), */N (values divisible by N), A-B (a range) and a plain number. The program should print true true false true false.
questions.explain: Check the special forms first: *, then */N with the remainder operator, then a range. What is left is a single number. A real cron parser also handles lists like 1,15 and names like mon.

questions.q: Simulate overlap: "skip" without timers. fireTimes are the minutes a job fires, and every run lasts duration minutes. Finish runStarts so it returns the fire times that really start a run: skip a fire time while the previous run is still going (a run that started at 0 with duration 25 is busy until minute 25). The program should print [ 0, 30, 60 ].
questions.explain: Remember when the current run ends. A fire time before that is dropped; otherwise it starts a run and moves busyUntil. The run at 0 blocks 10 and 20, the run at 30 blocks 40 and 50. With "allow", all seven would start and pile up.

questions.q: Two servers both fire the digest job. Finish handleDigest(scheduledAt) so the digest is sent at most once per day. Take the day from scheduledAt (the first 10 characters of its ISO string), remember sent days in sentDays, and return "sent" or "skipped". The program should print sent skipped sent.
questions.explain: The second Monday call is the duplicate from the other server and does nothing. Tuesday is a new day. In the real Task API, sentDays is a table with a unique day column, so the database refuses the second insert even across machines.

questions.q: On start, the app restores stored reminders. Finish restore(row, now, policy): if the reminder's time is still in the future, return its ISO time. If it already passed, return now as an ISO string for policy "run-once", or "skipped" for policy "skip". The program should print the three lines shown in the comments.
questions.explain: This is the misfire rule: a time in the future is kept; a missed time runs once right away with "run-once", or is refused with "skip". Comparing getTime() values compares instants, whatever the zone.

questions.q: Day names work in the day-of-week field. Starting from Friday 2 October 2026, what does this print?
questions.explain: sat,sun is a list: Saturday or Sunday. The next weekend days after Friday are Saturday 3 and Sunday 4, then Saturday 10 October.

questions.q: The clock is fixed at 12:00. What does this print?
questions.explain: After resume() the schedule is active again, and the next run is computed from now: 10 minutes after 12:00. Missed fire times are never replayed in a burst.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The data passed when scheduling reaches the handler as ctx.data, and ctx.jobId is the job's id (sync), not its human name (Sync).
